quiz.title: Unit 6 SAQ 01
quiz.headline: Mill on liberty and empire
quiz.prompt: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question.
quiz.instructions: Answer all three parts. For each part, Answer the question directly, Prove it with specific historical evidence, and Explain how the evidence supports your answer. On the AP exam each part earns one point. This is self-assessment practice, not official College Board scoring.
quiz.note: Original Page One practice in AP short-answer format. Model answers show one strong response; other accurate, well-supported answers can earn the point.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: John Stuart Mill, British philosopher and official of the East India Company from 1823 to 1858, On Liberty, 1859
stimulusBlocks.citation: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, ch. 1, Introductory. Project Gutenberg eBook #34901.
stimulusBlocks.note: “This doctrine” is Mill's principle that people should be free to act as they choose unless they harm others. “Nonage” means childhood or immaturity. Akbar was the Mughal emperor.
stimulusBlocks.text: It is, perhaps, hardly necessary to say that this doctrine is meant to apply only to human beings in the maturity of their faculties. . . . For the same reason, we may leave out of consideration those backward states of society in which the race itself may be considered as in its nonage. . . . Despotism is a legitimate mode of government in dealing with barbarians, provided the end be their improvement, and the means justified by actually effecting that end. Liberty, as a principle, has no application to any state of things anterior to the time when mankind have become capable of being improved by free and equal discussion. Until then, there is nothing for them but implicit obedience to an Akbar or a Charlemagne, if they are so fortunate as to find one.

scaffold.label: Answer
scaffold.text: Respond directly to the task verb: identify, describe, or explain.

scaffold.label: Prove
scaffold.text: Name a specific person, place, institution, or development.

scaffold.label: Explain
scaffold.text: Show how or why the evidence answers the question.

parts.prompt: Identify ONE claim Mill makes about which societies his principle of liberty applies to.
criteria: States a specific claim from the passage.
Connects it to who deserves liberty.

model.answer: Mill claims that liberty applies only to societies he considered mature or advanced.
model.prove: He writes that “Liberty, as a principle, has no application” until people can be improved “by free and equal discussion.”
model.explain: This lets Mill defend freedom in Britain while accepting despotic rule over peoples he labeled backward.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also identify his claim that despotism is legitimate over “barbarians” if the goal is their improvement.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE way European states put ideas like Mill's into practice in the period 1750 to 1900.
criteria: Names a specific colonial policy or region.
Explains how it reflected the idea of rule for improvement.

model.answer: Britain ruled India directly while claiming to improve it.
model.prove: After 1858 the British Crown governed India, building railways and introducing English-language education for an elite while denying Indians self-government.
model.explain: British officials presented these projects as progress, which echoes Mill's view that despotism was acceptable when aimed at improvement.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain mission schools and the civilizing mission in Africa, or the US justification for ruling the Philippines.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE way Mill's position or situation might have shaped his argument.
criteria: Identifies a specific feature of Mill's situation.
Explains how it shaped the passage.

model.answer: Mill worked for the East India Company for decades, so he had a stake in defending British rule in India.
model.prove: He served the company from 1823 to 1858, and in the passage he names the Mughal emperor Akbar as an example of a good despot.
model.explain: A man whose career depended on ruling India had reason to argue that rule without consent could be legitimate there.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain that Mill wrote as a British liberal in an age of imperial confidence, when ideas of European superiority were widespread.
